title: J. R. D. Tata Flies the First Mail From Karachi, Without a Subsidy
dek: Refused a mail subsidy twice, JRD Tata and Nevill Vintcent started India's first air service anyway, and JRD flew its opening leg himself on 15 October 1932.

story.founder: J. R. D. Tata (with Nevill Vintcent)
story.company: Tata Air Lines (Tata Aviation Service, later Air India)
story.event: Flying the first Tata airmail from Karachi to Bombay after the government refused a subsidy
story.summary: On 15 October 1932 J. R. D. Tata flew the first Tata airmail from Karachi to Bombay via Ahmedabad in a Puss Moth, and Nevill Vintcent, who had proposed the airline, flew the mail on to Madras. The government had twice refused a mail subsidy, so the service ran as a department of Tata Sons on a small initial investment and the senders' stamp surcharge. It completed its first year with 100 per cent punctuality and later became Air India.
paragraphs: At 6.30 on the morning of 15 October 1932, J. R. D. Tata shook hands with a small send-off party at Drigh Road aerodrome in Karachi, among them the city's postmaster, and took off alone in a two-seater de Havilland Puss Moth loaded with mail. The bags had come from London by Imperial Airways. At Ahmedabad petrol was brought to the plane by bullock cart. He landed on the mud flats at Juhu, outside Bombay, at 1.50 that afternoon, and within twenty minutes Nevill Vintcent was flying the Madras mail onward in a second Puss Moth.

The idea was Vintcent's. A former Royal Air Force pilot who had been giving joyrides around India, he brought JRD a plan for an airline; JRD had become the first Indian to qualify as a pilot in India in 1929. The chairman of Tata Sons, Sir Dorab Tata, was "not a bit enthusiastic," but the outlay was small, Rs 200,000 by the group's account, and JRD's mentor John Peterson talked him round. The service would run as a department of Tata Sons.

The government would not help. Tata asked for a small subsidy for carrying the mail, as was normal elsewhere, and was refused; it cut the figure to a bare minimum and was refused again. JRD and Vintcent went ahead on the little surcharge senders paid to have letters flown on from Karachi. Asked why, JRD said they believed "if we came in at the beginning of an era we had a better chance ultimately to achieve growth and leadership in the field." There was no radio and no aerodrome in Bombay, he recalled. In the monsoon Juhu went under water, and the whole outfit, two planes, three pilots and three mechanics, moved to Poona.

A hundred days later JRD told the Rotary Club of Bombay that "a few lean years will precede the great development that must come." Its first year ended on 10 October 1933 with 100 per cent punctuality, monsoon included, the Directorate of Civil Aviation reported. By 1934, Flight magazine reported, it was showing a profit. Revenue rose sharply after 1936, when Britain began flying first-class mail without surcharge. The airline became Air India in 1946. Vintcent had gone missing in 1942 aboard an RAF Hudson.

quote.text: Not a victory is gained, not a deed of faithfulness or courage is done, except upon a maybe; not a service, not a sally of generosity, not a scientific exploration or experiment or text-book, that may not be a mistake.
quote.work: Is Life Worth Living?, in The Will to Believe, and Other Essays in Popular Philosophy (1897)
quote.locator: "Is Life Worth Living?", p. 59 of the 1897 edition
quote.source_title: The Will to Believe, and Other Essays in Popular Philosophy, Project Gutenberg eBook #26659
quote.connection: James holds that nothing worth doing is done except on a maybe that could still prove a mistake. JRD's unsubsidised mail service was a maybe of exactly that kind; a punctual first year and the 1936 mail scheme made it look wise, but nothing promised either in October 1932.

reflection: You may be waiting for some kind of backing before you let yourself begin properly: a grant, a partner, a first signed contract. JRD asked twice and was refused twice. What he did next was modest rather than heroic. He found the smallest version of the service that could pay its own way, and he said in public that lean years would come first.

Saying that out loud matters. It keeps an ordinary lean year from feeling like a verdict on you, and it lets the people around you, at work and at home, know what kind of years to expect, so that they can plan their own lives around yours.
invitation: Write one sentence describing the smallest version of your work that could run without the support you are still waiting for. Show it to no one yet; keep it where you will see it tomorrow.

sources.title: Song of the Clouds (excerpt from R. M. Lala, Beyond the Last Blue Mountain, July 2023)
sources.supports: Opening postponed from 15 September 1932 because Juhu was flooded; 6.30 a.m. take-off from Drigh Road, Karachi, on 15 October 1932 after shaking hands with the send-off party including the Postmaster of Karachi; refuelling at Ahmedabad with petrol brought by bullock cart; landing in Bombay at 1.50 p.m.; Vintcent taking the Madras and Bellary mail on within twenty minutes in a second Puss Moth; JRD's Rotary Club speech a hundred days later ('A few lean years will precede the great development that must come'); 1933-34 Directorate of Civil Aviation praise

sources.title: Wings for a Nation
sources.supports: Vintcent, a former RAF officer who had been giving joyrides, offering JRD the airline project; Sir Dorab Tata 'not a bit enthusiastic'; initial investment of Rs 200,000; John Peterson persuading Sir Dorab; Karachi chosen because Imperial Airways ended there; two requests for a small mail subsidy refused; running the service on the stamp surcharge; JRD's 'if we came in at the beginning of an era we had a better chance ultimately to achieve growth and leadership in the field'; no radio, aids or aerodrome in Bombay; Juhu mud flat flooded in the monsoon and the move to Poona with two planes, three pilots and three mechanics; DCA report of 100 per cent punctuality for the year to 10 October 1933; revenues rising after the 1936 Empire Mail Service; Air-India in 1946

sources.title: Tata group and Air India: the beginnings (R. P. Narla, Tata Central Archives)
sources.supports: Air-mail operations to be run as a departmental operation of Tata Sons with Sir Dorabji Tata's approval; the Puss Moths bought in England; renamed Tata Airlines in 1938 and Air India Ltd in July 1946

sources.title: When air mail came to Madras (Madras Musings, Vol. XX No. 14, 1-15 November 2010)
sources.supports: Service began on 15 October 1932 on the route Karachi-Ahmedabad-Bombay-Bellary-Madras, connecting with Imperial Airways' London-Karachi flight; mail bags had left London a week earlier; JRD flew Karachi to Bombay in a Puss Moth and Vintcent flew on to Madras; investment given as Rs 1 lakh

sources.title: The making of J.R.D. Tata's legacy, which has come back home (8 October 2021)
sources.supports: Launch on 15 October 1932; Vintcent, a former RAF pilot, and Sir Dorabji's initial reluctance; Rs 200,000 to set up the airline; second-hand two-seater Puss Moth flown via Ahmedabad to Bombay and on to Madras; Karachi chosen as the end of the Imperial Airways route; JRD's licence on 10 February 1929 as the first Indian to get one in India; Juhu and the monsoon move to Poona; DCA 1933-34 praise

cross_checks.claim: JRD Tata flew the first Tata airmail from Karachi to Bombay via Ahmedabad on 15 October 1932, and Vintcent flew the mail on to Madras.
Karachi was the starting point because Imperial Airways' mail service from London ended there.
Sir Dorab Tata was reluctant and the initial investment was Rs 200,000.
The service ran without a government subsidy.
The first year ended in October 1933 with 100 per cent punctuality.

research_notes: Investment: Rs 200,000 (Tata's 'Wings for a Nation'; DT Next) versus Rs 1 lakh (Madras Musings); the story gives Rs 200,000 attributed to the group's own account. Mail load: Lala gives 55 lb for Bombay and 8 lb left at Ahmedabad, with Vintcent taking 47 lb for Madras and 6 lb for Bellary (together about 116 lb, consistent with other reports of 'more than 100 pounds'); a 25 kg figure also circulates; the story gives no weight. Madras arrival: 16 October (A Fleeting Peace, which also routes Vintcent via Bangalore) versus 17 October after a night at Bellary (Madras Musings); the story does not date it. Aircraft registration is given as VT-AND (Madras Musings) or VT-ACZ (other philatelic pages); not used. The 1929 proposal: Tata's archives page says J. S. Newall and Vintcent proposed a Karachi-Madras air mail on 19 March 1929, while 'Wings for a Nation' credits Vintcent alone; the story credits Vintcent, as JRD did. JRD's licence date (10 February 1929) is from DT Next; the story says 1929 only. The Flight 1934 remark on profit is quoted on A Fleeting Peace, a golden-age aviation history site, and is attributed to Flight. Vintcent's death: A Fleeting Peace gives Hudson AM946 lost on 29 January 1942, 'missing believed killed'; Tata says the aircraft was reportedly shot down off France; the story says he went missing. Funding kept as 'mixed': the service was a department of Tata Sons funded from group money and run on the postal surcharge, with no government subsidy. Spelling follows the sources' 'Vintcent'. JRD quotations are taken from Tata's heritage pages (which reproduce his recollections and Lala's biography) and checked against the page text. The James passage is from the essay 'Is Life Worth Living?' (an 1895 address, collected in 1897).
